title: Inference as a Production Fabric — one-pager
executive_summary: Short, product-focused narrative to use in product one-pagers and sales enablement: Redwood is the production fabric that lets engineering teams stitch LLM capabilities into products with predictable latency, costs, and operational controls. This brief frames ‘why Redwood’ in operational terms that matter to platform builders and product leads.
mission_statement: Make inference a predictable, auditable, and economical substrate for product teams so that feature velocity is measured in shipped experiences, not model maintenance.
thesis: As models commoditize, the sustainable advantage moves to the quality of serving. Teams succeed when they can run reliable inference at scale with transparent economics, graceful degradation, and consistent developer ergonomics — not just by picking the best model. Redwood is built as that serving fabric.
why_redwood: Redwood unifies runtime performance, observability, and operational controls across hosted, reserved, and private deployments. Engineers get a single API and tooling that reduces surprises: token-level cost visibility, rollout controls, deterministic fallbacks, and optimized execution paths so customers can ship features with SLOs, not gamble on model throughput.
key_messages: Serving is the new product boundary: the difference between a prototype and a production feature is predictable inference.
Transparent unit economics: per-token visibility and actionable levers (batching, caching, quantization) that move dollars and latency, not opaque knobs.
Operational-first design: fallbacks, model variants, and rollout policies that keep customer-facing features online during outages or regressions.
One interface across environments: same API and observability whether hosted, dedicated, or private — reduces ops friction and lock-in risk.
Developer ergonomics at scale: SDKs, eval hooks, and cost-aware defaults so engineering teams can iterate quickly without compromising SLOs.
target_audiences: Platform and infrastructure teams evaluating inference options for multiple product orgs
Product engineers building LLM-powered features who need latency and cost guarantees
GTM and solutions teams positioning Redwood for enterprise deals with compliance or private deployments
competitive_differentiators: Runtime-first economics: we surface the direct ROI levers (batching, cache, quantization) and automate safe defaults; competitors offer either model access or raw infra, not the economics layer.
Fallback and rollout primitives: automatic model variant routing and canary behaviors tuned for response quality and SLOs — most providers lack integrated fallback policies.
Unified deployment surface: identical API and observability across hosted, dedicated, and VPC/on-prem deployments removes a major migration friction point.
Instrumented regressions: tie quality regressions to prompt sets and traffic slices so teams can detect and revert before customers notice.
usage_examples: SaaS product embeds assistant: uses dedicated pools and prefix caching to hit aggressive latency SLOs for interactive workflows while reducing per-token spend by 30%.
Regulated enterprise: private deployment + KMS + audit logs so sensitive data never leaves customer network, with the same rollout controls used in hosted mode.
Marketplace recommender: intelligent batching and model-variant fallbacks to preserve throughput during peak traffic spikes without overprovisioning.
go_to_market_signal: Use this brief in sales discovery and product marketing where the buyer cares about operational risk, predictable TCO, and cross-environment consistency. Primary call-to-action: run a low-friction proof-of-concept that validates latency SLOs and unit economics on customer workloads.
